text: Poultry disease recognition should focus on detecting unusual flock-level changes early, while recognizing that several diseases share symptoms. Newcastle disease (ជំងឺញូកាសល) can cause coughing, sneezing, breathing difficulty, diarrhea, tremors, paralysis, twisted necks, circling, reduced/abnormal egg production, or an unusual rise in deaths, and can spread rapidly. Avian influenza (ជំងឺផ្តាសាយបក្សី) ranges from mild illness to sudden death with high mortality depending on strain -- sudden unexplained deaths should never be casually dismissed as ordinary illness. Infectious bronchitis causes coughing, sneezing, watery eyes, and reduced growth or egg production. Coccidiosis causes reduced appetite, poor growth, ruffled feathers, diarrhea, and sometimes significant mortality, worsened by wet, dirty litter. Critically, symptoms CANNOT reliably distinguish Newcastle disease from avian influenza -- never tell a farmer a flock 'definitely has' one of these based on a description. During the wet season, watch wet litter, mud, poor ventilation, and contact with wild birds; during the dry season, heat stress and crowding around water sources add risk, but heat stress and infectious disease can occur together, so don't attribute all mortality to heat without investigation. Practical smallholder priority: notice sudden changes in mortality, feed/water intake, egg production, or breathing; separate sick birds where feasible; avoid unnecessary movement/mixing; escalate sudden unexplained deaths or severe respiratory/neurological disease to a veterinarian or animal-health authority promptly for investigation and testing.
